blocks.text: 2.14	How much energy is required to ionise a H atom if  the electron occupies n = 5 orbit? Compare your answer with the ionization enthalpy of H atom (energy required to remove the electron from n =1 orbit).
2.15	What is the maximum number of emission lines when the excited electron of a H atom in n = 6 drops to the ground state?

2.16	(i)	 The energy associated with the first orbit in the hydrogen atom is –2.18 × 10–18 J atom–1. What is the energy associated with the fifth orbit?
	(ii) Calculate the radius of Bohr’s fifth orbit for hydrogen atom.
2.17	Calculate the wavenumber for the longest wavelength transition in the Balmer series of atomic hydrogen.

2.18	What is the energy in joules, required to shift the electron of the hydrogen atom from the first Bohr orbit to the fifth Bohr orbit and what is the wavelength of the light emitted when the electron returns to the ground state? The ground state electron energy is –2.18 × 10–11 ergs.

2.19	The electron energy in hydrogen atom is given by En = (–2.18 × 10–18 )/n2 J. Calculate the energy required to remove an electron completely from the n = 2 orbit. What is the longest wavelength of light in cm that can be used to cause this transition?
2.20	Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 2.05 × 107 m s–1.
2.21	The mass of an electron is 9.1 × 10–31 kg. If its K.E. is 3.0 × 10–25 J, calculate its wavelength.

2.22	Which of the following are isoelectronic species  i.e., those having the same number of electrons?
			Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, S2–, Ar.

2.23 	(i) Write the electronic configurations of the following ions: (a) H– (b) Na+ (c) O2– (d) F–
	(ii)	 What are the atomic numbers of elements whose outermost electrons are represented by (a) 3s1 (b) 2p3 and (c) 3p5 ?
	(iii) Which atoms are indicated by the following configurations ?
		(a) [He] 2s1  (b) [Ne] 3s2 3p3  (c) [Ar] 4s2 3d1.
2.24	What is the lowest value of n that allows g orbitals to exist?
2.25	An electron is in one of the 3d orbitals. Give the possible values of n, l  and ml for this electron.
2.26 	An atom of an element contains 29 electrons and 35 neutrons. Deduce (i) the number of protons and (ii) the electronic configuration of the element.
2.27	Give the number of electrons in the species

2.28	(i)	 An atomic orbital has n = 3. What are the possible values of l and ml ?
	(ii)	 List the quantum numbers (ml and l) of electrons for 3d orbital.
	(iii) 	Which of the following orbitals are possible?
	 	1p, 2s, 2p and 3f

2.29	Using s, p, d notations, describe the orbital with the following quantum numbers.
	(a) n=1, l=0; (b) n = 3; l=1 (c) n = 4; l =2; (d) n=4; l=3.

2.30	Explain, giving reasons, which of the following sets of quantum numbers are not possible.
		 (a) 	 n = 0, 	 	l = 0,		ml  =   0,	ms = + ½
		 (b) 	 n = 1, 	 	l = 0,		ml  =   0, 	ms = – ½
		 (c) 	 n = 1, 	 	l = 1,		ml  =   0,	ms = + ½
		 (d) 	 n = 2, 	 	l = 1,		ml  =   0, 	ms = – ½

note: Seam judged against CHE11L-ch02-p041.runA.json, written immediately before this page (the instruction's named anchor p030 has no output on disk). p041's last block is exercise 2.13, a complete question ending in '?', and its last_block_continues_on_next is false; this page opens with a fresh item, 2.14, so first_block_continues_from_previous is false and the two pages agree. input's previous_page_last_block was null. last_block_continues_on_next is TRUE, and this one needs saying plainly because the page LOOKS like it ends on a tidy complete item: exercise 2.30's answer-set list is cut off after row (d), and p043's text layer opens with ' (e)\tn = 3, l = 3, ml  = –3, ms = + ½' and ' (f)\tn = 3, l = 1, ml  =   0, ms = + ½' — rows (e) and (f) of this very same 2.30 — before reaching 2.31. So block n=18 continues onto p043, and p043 must set first_block_continues_from_previous true. The whole page is the single-column continuation of the EXERCISES section, items 2.14 to 2.30, each numbered exercise taken as one list block with its roman and lettered sub-parts inside it, in the printed order the text layer also uses; there is no heading, figure or table on the page and the lower sixth is blank. Block n=15 is the ONLY deferral, and it is the one place on the page where the layer has lost content outright: exercise 2.27 asks for the electron count of three species, printed as H-two-plus, H-two and O-two-plus with their charges as superscripts and their 2s as subscripts, and the text layer stores the item as 'Give the number of electrons in the species ' and then NOTHING — all three species are absent from it, not merely scrambled. So block n=14 carries the item's prose exactly as far as the layer has it and block n=15 gives the species group a bbox with empty text for the special transcriber. Everywhere else the inline quantities follow the layer's own flattened spelling rather than the printed superscripts: '–2.18 × 10–18 J atom–1', '–2.18 × 10–11 ergs', 'given by En = (–2.18 × 10–18 )/n2 J.' (the layer's flattening of E-sub-n and of the printed /n-squared, with its space before the closing bracket), 'velocity of 2.05 × 107 m s–1.' (its flattening of 2.05 × 10-to-the-7), '9.1 × 10–31 kg', '3.0 × 10–25 J', 'Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, S2–, Ar.', '(a) H– (b) Na+ (c) O2– (d) F–', '(a) 3s1 (b) 2p3 and (c) 3p5 ?', '(a) [He] 2s1  (b) [Ne] 3s2 3p3  (c) [Ar] 4s2 3d1.', 'values of n, l  and ml', and the 'ml' and 'ms' of 2.28 and 2.30. Spelled with superscripts these would fold into numbers the page never prints. The doubled spaces ('a H atom if  the electron', 'isoelectronic species  i.e.,', 'values of n, l  and ml', '[He] 2s1  (b)', 'ml  =   0'), the missing space in 'from n =1 orbit' and the tab indents are the layer's and the page's own and are not tidied. Unicode one-half glyphs in 2.30 are as printed. bboxes are original-image pixels (1750x2180); the image renders at 1606x2000, so displayed coordinates were scaled by 1.09.
